title: JESUS SAID, “DO NOT SWEAR AT ALL.” SO WHY ARE CHRISTIANS STILL TAKING OATHS?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “DO NOT SWEAR AT ALL.” SO WHY ARE CHRISTIANS STILL TAKING OATHS?
The unsettling truth behind Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12—and the question every believer must answer before placing a hand on the Bible and promising to tell the truth.
Imagine standing inside a courtroom.
The room falls silent. Your family is watching. A judge is waiting. Someone asks you to raise your right hand and swear that what you are about to say is the truth.
Your heart begins to pound.
Not because you intend to lie.
But because you remember something Jesus said.
“But I say unto you, Swear not at all.” — Matthew 5:34 (KJV)
Not swear carefully.
Not swear only when the circumstances are serious.
Not swear as long as you are holding a Bible.
Jesus said, “Swear not at all.”
And suddenly, what seemed like a simple legal procedure becomes a deeply personal question of obedience.
Would you be disobeying Christ if you took that oath?
Would refusing it mean you were honoring Him?
And what about Christians who have already sworn marriage vows, taken oaths of office, testified under oath, or made solemn promises before God?
Have they sinned without realizing it?
Before you rush to answer, there is something you need to understand.
This is not merely a question about what Christians are allowed to say. It is a question about what kind of people Jesus died to make us.
And somewhere inside His words is a truth that may expose something far more serious than an oath.
Something about the way we speak.
The way we promise.
The way we hide.
And the way we sometimes use God's name to make people believe words our character has not earned.
Because the real scandal may not be that Christians take oaths.
The real scandal may be that we have become so comfortable with dishonesty that people sometimes need an oath before they can trust us.
And Jesus came to change that.
In Matthew 5, Jesus is preaching what we call the Sermon on the Mount.

He is not giving His followers a collection of clever religious sayings. He is describing the righteousness of the kingdom of heaven—a righteousness that reaches beyond outward religious performance and confronts the human heart.
He has already spoken about anger, lust, reconciliation, and faithfulness.
Now He turns to the words that come out of our mouths.
He says:
“Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths:
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:
Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.
Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.”
— Matthew 5:33–37 (KJV)
Those words are sharper than many of us realize.
To understand why, we need to go back.
Long before Jesus preached on that mountain, the Law of Moses had already condemned false swearing.
Leviticus 19:12 declares:
“And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.”
Numbers 30:2 teaches that a person who makes a vow or binds himself by an oath must not break his word.
Deuteronomy 23:21–23 likewise warns against failing to fulfill a vow made to the LORD.
The Old Testament did not treat oaths as meaningless religious decorations.
An oath was serious because God's name was serious.
To invoke His name was to acknowledge that the living God was witness to what a person said.
Truth was never supposed to be optional.
But human beings have a remarkable ability to take something holy and turn it into a loophole.
By the time Jesus addressed the subject, some religious distinctions concerning oaths had become dangerously misleading.
Matthew 23:16–22 exposes the problem.
Jesus rebuked religious guides who distinguished between swearing by the temple and swearing by the gold of the temple, as though certain formulas carried greater binding force than others.
Think about what that meant.
A person could become more concerned about the exact words of an oath than whether those words were true.
The language sounded religious.
The heart remained dishonest.
And Jesus refused to let that hypocrisy survive unchallenged.
When He said not to swear by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or even one's own head, He was dismantling the illusion that human beings could separate ordinary speech from God's authority.
Heaven is God's throne.
Earth is His footstool.
Jerusalem belongs to the great King.
And your own head?
You cannot even control the natural color of a single hair.
In other words, you do not possess the authority you sometimes pretend to possess.
You cannot make yourself the ultimate guarantee of tomorrow.
You cannot control every outcome.
You cannot force the future to obey your promises.
And you cannot escape God's presence by choosing a supposedly less sacred object for your oath.
Every word you speak is already spoken before God.
That is where the teaching begins to become uncomfortable.
Because we may never have stood in a courtroom and sworn falsely.
But how many times have we said, “I promise,” knowing we had little intention of following through?
How many times have we said, “God knows I'm telling the truth,” while carefully withholding the part of the story that would expose us?
How many times have we used spiritual language to strengthen our credibility instead of allowing honesty to establish it?
A husband says, “I swear I'll never do it again.”
A wife hears the same promise she heard last month.
A parent promises to change.
A child waits.
A friend says, “Trust me this time.”
But the trust has already been broken.
And somewhere in the wreckage of those relationships, Jesus speaks.
Let your yes be yes.
Let your no be no.
Not because words are unimportant.
But because words are so important that they should not require a religious performance to become truthful.
Now we need to examine something that is often missed when people quote Matthew 5:34.
The New Testament was written in Greek, and the wording matters.
The phrase translated “Swear not at all” is:
μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως
Transliterated: mē omosai holōs.
A faithful rendering is: “Do not swear at all.”
The Greek verb omnyō, from which omosai comes, refers to swearing an oath.
Jesus is not merely prohibiting vulgar language or profanity, although Scripture addresses corrupt speech elsewhere.
He is addressing oath-taking.
And the word holōs intensifies the statement.
It means “at all” or “altogether.”
We should not soften that language simply because it makes us uncomfortable.
Jesus really did speak in sweeping terms.
But faithful interpretation requires more than reading one phrase in isolation.
We must ask how the statement functions within the entire Sermon on the Mount, how it relates to the rest of Scripture, and how the earliest Christians understood the seriousness of His command.
This is where sincere believers have reached different conclusions.
And we should be careful not to accuse fellow Christians of rebellion simply because they interpret this difficult passage differently.
Some Christian traditions understand Jesus to prohibit all oath-taking, including judicial oaths.
Anabaptist traditions, including Mennonites and other historic peace-church communities, have often emphasized this reading.
For them, Jesus' words are direct and comprehensive.
If Christ says not to swear at all, the disciple should not swear.
Instead, a believer should simply affirm the truth.
That conviction deserves serious respect.
It is not necessarily a rejection of government, justice, or responsibility.
It can arise from a sincere desire to obey the plain words of Jesus.
Other Christian traditions understand the passage as condemning manipulative, deceptive, unnecessary, or casual oath-taking rather than every solemn oath made for a legitimate purpose.
They point to other passages where solemn appeals to God appear without explicit condemnation.
And those passages deserve equally careful examination.
Consider Hebrews 6:13.
“For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself.”
The writer continues by explaining the significance of God's oath in confirming His promise.
Hebrews 6:16 says:
“For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife.”
The passage describes an oath as a recognized means of confirmation.
More importantly, it presents God's own oath as an expression of His unchanging purpose.
Of course, God is not a sinful human being who needs to overcome dishonesty.
He cannot lie.
His oath is not evidence that He lacks credibility.
It is an act of gracious assurance toward human beings who need encouragement.
And that distinction matters.
We cannot simply say, “God swore an oath, therefore Christians may swear any oath they choose.”
That would be careless reasoning.
But neither can we ignore the fact that Scripture portrays solemn oath language in contexts that are not inherently sinful.
Consider the apostle Paul.
In 2 Corinthians 1:23, he writes:
Paul is calling upon God as witness to the truth of his explanation.
In Galatians 1:20, he writes:
And in Romans 1:9, he declares:
“For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son…”
These are solemn appeals to God's knowledge.
They are not necessarily identical in form to a modern courtroom oath, but they demonstrate that Paul could invoke God as witness while speaking truthfully.
Then there is the trial of Jesus Himself.
In Matthew 26:63, the high priest says:
“I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God.”
The Greek expression includes the verb ἐξορκίζω (exorkizō), meaning to put someone under oath or solemnly charge someone.
The high priest invokes the living God in demanding an answer.
Jesus responds:
“Thou hast said…”
He then speaks of the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power and coming in the clouds of heaven.
This passage is significant, but we must interpret it honestly.
It does not explicitly say that Jesus recited an oath formula.
Nor does it record Him commanding His disciples to take oaths.
It shows Him responding truthfully when solemnly charged before the high priest.
Therefore, it contributes to the discussion without settling every question by itself.
And that is an important principle.
We do not honor Scripture by forcing a passage to prove more than it actually says.
Sometimes the most faithful words a Bible teacher can speak are, “Christians have understood this differently, and we must examine the evidence carefully.”
Because biblical conviction should be built on truth, not on the confidence of the person holding the microphone.
Then James enters the conversation.
And his words sound unmistakably like the words of Jesus.
“But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.”
— James 5:12 (KJV)
The Greek phrase translated “do not swear” is:
μὴ ὀμνύετε
Transliterated: mē omnyete.
It is a direct prohibition against swearing.
James continues with language closely resembling Matthew 5:37.
His concern is not merely etiquette.
It is spiritual accountability.
A believer's speech should be truthful, dependable, and free from deceptive manipulation.
James has already warned that the tongue can become a destructive fire.
He has described the contradiction of blessing God while cursing human beings made in God's likeness.
He knows that spiritual maturity is revealed not only in what people believe but also in what they say.
And here is something worth noticing.
James does not tell believers to develop more impressive ways of promising.
He tells them to become people whose ordinary words can be trusted.
There is something deeply convicting about that.
Because many of us want God to bless our testimony while we refuse to let Him confront our dishonesty.
We want spiritual authority without personal integrity.
We want people to trust us because we quote Scripture.
But Jesus calls us to become trustworthy because His truth has transformed us.
And perhaps that is why this teaching cuts so deeply.
It removes our hiding places.
You cannot cover a lie with a Bible verse.
You cannot sanctify deception by saying, “God is my witness.”
You cannot make a broken promise holy simply because you made it in church.
You cannot deceive someone privately and expect public worship to erase the damage.
Jesus is not impressed by religious language that conceals an unrepentant heart.
He is calling His people into the light.
But we still have to answer the practical question.
Can a Christian take an oath in court?

The most responsible answer is that faithful Christians disagree about whether Jesus prohibits every formal oath or primarily condemns the deceptive oath practices and careless swearing addressed in His teaching.
A Christian who believes all oath-taking is forbidden should not violate that conviction merely to satisfy social expectations.
Romans 14:23 teaches that acting against faith is spiritually serious, although Paul's immediate discussion concerns disputable practices involving food.
In many legal systems, a person may make a solemn affirmation instead of taking a religious oath, though the exact rules depend on the jurisdiction.
An affirmation is not permission to be less truthful.
It carries a serious obligation to speak honestly, and false statements may still bring legal consequences.
A Christian who understands solemn judicial oaths to be permissible must likewise recognize that invoking God's name is never a casual matter.
An oath must never become an excuse for dishonesty, exaggeration, concealment, or false testimony.
Exodus 20:7 warns against taking the name of the LORD in vain.
Exodus 20:16 prohibits bearing false witness against one's neighbor.
And Proverbs 12:22 declares:
“Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.”
Whether someone swears an oath or makes an affirmation, lying remains sin.
Whether a person raises a hand or keeps it lowered, truth remains sacred.
Whether the words are spoken inside a courtroom, around a dinner table, in a business meeting, or through a private message, the disciple of Jesus is accountable for what comes out of the mouth.
What about marriage vows?
Here, too, we should distinguish between solemn promises and the precise issue of invoking an oath.
Scripture treats marriage as a covenant of profound seriousness.
Malachi 2:14 describes the wife as a man's companion and wife by covenant.
Ephesians 5:25 calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church.
Marriage promises are not automatically identical to the oath formulas Jesus criticizes in Matthew 5.
Some Christians are comfortable making solemn wedding vows before God.
Others prefer covenantal promises without oath language.
The crucial issue is not whether the ceremony sounds impressive.
It is whether the promises reflect sincere faithfulness.
Because a beautiful wedding vow cannot compensate for a life of betrayal.
And a simple promise can carry extraordinary weight when it is honored through sacrifice, repentance, patience, and love.
What about an oath of office, military oath, professional oath, or citizenship oath?
Christians should examine both the wording and the obligations involved.
No oath can legitimately require a believer to sin against God.
Acts 5:29 declares:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
If an oath demands unconditional loyalty that would override obedience to Christ, the believer has a serious reason to refuse or seek an appropriate alternative.

But if an oath concerns truthful testimony, lawful service, or responsible fulfillment of legitimate duties, Christians will evaluate its permissibility according to their understanding of Scripture and conscience.

The important thing is to refuse the easy escape of treating every oath as automatically righteous because society approves it—or automatically wicked without examining the relevant biblical arguments.
Jesus deserves more than a rushed answer.
He deserves our careful attention.
But now I want to bring this closer.
Away from the courtroom.
Away from the theological debate.
Away from Greek vocabulary and historical arguments.
I want you to imagine someone who trusted you.
Someone who believed your words.
Someone who defended your character when others doubted you.
Someone who looked into your eyes and believed you would never betray them.
And then you did.
Maybe it was a lie.
Maybe it was an affair.
Maybe it was money you promised to return.
Maybe it was a secret you swore you would protect.
Maybe it was an addiction you insisted you had conquered.
Maybe it was a promise to your children that you repeatedly broke.
Or perhaps you were the one betrayed.
You remember the words.
“I swear.”
“I promise.”
“You can trust me.”
And you remember what happened afterward.
Sometimes the deepest wounds are not caused by strangers.
They are caused by people whose words once made us feel safe.
This is why truthfulness matters so much to God.
Lies do not merely distort information.
They can destroy trust, fracture families, manipulate the vulnerable, and leave people questioning whether love itself can be believed.
And when Christians lie while claiming to represent Christ, the damage can reach even further.
People may begin to associate the name of Jesus with the hypocrisy of those who misused it.
That is a tragedy.
But listen carefully.
Your failure to keep your word does not mean Jesus has failed to keep His.
Human promises may collapse.
His faithfulness does not.
People may deceive you.
Christ remains true.
And if you are the one who lied, betrayed, manipulated, or broke a promise, the Gospel does not tell you to keep pretending.
It calls you to repent.
Not to defend the lie.
Not to rename the sin.
Not to blame the person who discovered it.
Not to hide behind the sentence, “Nobody is perfect.”
But to come into the light.
To confess what you have done.
To stop the deception.
To accept responsibility.
To make restitution where possible.
To rebuild trust through consistent action rather than demanding instant forgiveness from those you have hurt.
And to remember that forgiveness does not automatically erase every earthly consequence.
This is not hopelessness.
This is where real restoration begins.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the foundation of that promise.
God's faithfulness.
Not ours.
His righteousness.
Not our performance.
His grace.
Not our ability to construct a convincing excuse.
And now we arrive at the most beautiful truth in this entire discussion.
Jesus never needed to lie to save Himself.
Think about that.
He stood before religious authorities who sought His condemnation.
He faced accusations.
He endured humiliation.
He was mocked, beaten, and eventually crucified.
He could have denied who He was.
He could have manipulated His testimony to escape suffering.
But He did not.
First Peter 2:22 says of Christ:
“Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
The Greek word translated “guile” is δόλος (dolos).
It refers to deceit or treachery.
No deceit was found in His mouth.
Not a little.
Not occasionally.
Not when the pressure became unbearable.
Jesus was truthful when truthfulness was costly.
And that makes His sacrifice even more astonishing.
The One who never lied died for liars.
The One who never betrayed anyone gave His life for betrayers.
The One who perfectly fulfilled the Father's will carried the sins of people who had broken promises to God and to one another.
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
That does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
It means the sinless Christ bore our sin in His saving work so that those united to Him might be made righteous in Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not that God ignores dishonesty.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Not that grace gives us permission to continue manipulating people.
But that Jesus Christ, through His death and resurrection, offers forgiveness and a transformed life to sinners who turn to Him in faith.
The cross exposes the seriousness of our sin.
And the cross reveals the astonishing depth of God's mercy.
This is where scandal meets grace.
This is where shame no longer has to become your permanent identity.
This is where a person who once used words to deceive can learn to use words to heal.
Not because they have suddenly become perfect.
But because the Spirit of God is changing them.
Ephesians 4:25 says:
“Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.”
And Colossians 3:9–10 calls believers to put away lying because they have put off the old self and put on the new.
Christian truthfulness is not merely a rule imposed upon us.
It is part of the new life Christ is forming within us.
That transformation may be slow.
It may require difficult conversations.
It may involve confessing things we hoped nobody would discover.
It may require professional help, wise pastoral counsel, accountability, and patient restoration of damaged relationships.
But grace is not the enemy of truth.
Grace gives us the courage to face the truth without believing that our sin must have the final word.
So what should you do the next time someone asks you to swear an oath?
Study the Scriptures carefully.
Consider the command of Jesus without watering it down.
Examine the examples of solemn appeals to God without exaggerating what they prove.
Respect the consciences of sincere believers who reach a different conclusion.
Where an affirmation is available and better reflects your convictions, consider using it.
And never use any interpretation of this passage as an excuse to avoid telling the truth.
But perhaps the more important question is what you will do the next time you are tempted to lie.
When honesty might cost you money.
When confession might expose your reputation.
When telling the truth might end a relationship built on deception.
When keeping your promise requires sacrifice.
When you have the opportunity to make yourself look innocent by allowing someone else to carry the blame.
Will your yes still mean yes?
Will your no still mean no?
Will your commitment to Jesus remain when truth becomes expensive?
Because that is where discipleship becomes real.
Not only when we are defending Scripture in public.
But when we are obeying Christ in private.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past that conviction.
Perhaps there is someone you need to apologize to.
Perhaps there is a promise you need to stop making because you have no intention of keeping it.
Perhaps there is a lie you need to confess.
Perhaps there is someone whose trust you need to rebuild patiently, without pressuring them to heal on your timetable.
Or perhaps you are the wounded person who needs to hear that another person's dishonesty does not define your worth.
Jesus sees what happened.
He knows the truth.
And He has not abandoned the brokenhearted.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose another person's sin publicly.
But your honest response may encourage someone else who has been silently carrying the same struggle.
Do you believe Jesus prohibited every formal oath, or do you believe His primary concern was deceptive and unnecessary swearing?
Share the biblical passages that shape your conviction.
Let us disagree with humility where necessary, without losing the love that should identify us as followers of Christ.
Because a community that loves biblical truth should never be afraid of careful biblical discussion.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Think of the friend who has been betrayed.
The believer who is struggling with secret dishonesty.
The husband or wife trying to rebuild a marriage.
The young Christian trying to understand what obedience to Jesus really means.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, honest conviction, encouragement, repentance, healing, and above all, Jesus Christ.
Not a place where we merely collect religious information.
A place where the Word of God challenges how we actually live.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, understand their faith, strengthen their spiritual lives, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
And if you have been wondering how you can help this ministry continue reaching people, there is another way.
If you have been looking for a ministry to support as part of your Christian generosity, you may prayerfully consider this work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of fear.
Not because God's blessing can be purchased.
Not because you must pay to prove that you love Jesus.
But because the Gospel is worth sharing, biblical discipleship is worth supporting, and generosity can help sustain faithful ministry.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Use the free discipleship resources.
Keep growing in Christ.
Because the mission has never been to sell access to God's grace.
The mission is to proclaim the grace that Jesus has already purchased with His blood.
And as we return to the original question, perhaps we can finally see why Jesus' words matter so deeply.
Can Christians take oaths?
Faithful believers continue to differ about the scope of His prohibition.
But there is something no faithful reading of Matthew 5:33–37 or James 5:12 can reasonably deny.
Jesus calls His people to radical truthfulness.
He calls us away from deception.
Away from manipulative promises.
Away from religious language used to disguise unfaithfulness.
Away from the exhausting habit of becoming one person in public and another in private.
He calls us to become people whose words reflect the character of the Savior we follow.
And perhaps tonight, the most important oath is not one you are being asked to take.
Perhaps it is a promise you need to stop pretending you have kept.
Perhaps it is a confession you have been avoiding.
Perhaps it is a simple, trembling prayer:

“Lord Jesus, I have not always been truthful. I have broken promises. I have hidden things. I have sometimes cared more about protecting my reputation than honoring You. Forgive me. Teach me to speak the truth, even when it costs me. Give me courage to confess what I have done, humility to repair what I can, and grace to become someone whose words reflect Your faithfulness. Thank You for dying for sinners like me and rising again. Change my heart, Lord. Let my yes mean yes, and my no mean no. In Your name, Amen.”
You do not have to make a dramatic public oath to begin walking in obedience.
You can begin with the truth.
And when you fail, do not hide from the Savior who already knows.
Return to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the One who calls you into the light is the same One who gave His life to bring sinners out of darkness.
The most powerful testimony is not that you never broke your word—but that Jesus kept His, even when saving you cost Him everything.
